title: Planetary nebula Abell 39
caption: The planetary nebula Abell 39, imaged by the WIYN 3.5-meter Telescope

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This picture shows Abell 39, a planetary nebula with rare and beautiful spherical symmetry, in the constellation Hercules. The name comes from its place as number 39 in George Abell's 1966 catalog of large nebulae he had discovered.

A planetary nebula is the shell of gas cast off by a Sun-like star late in its life. The name is historical and has nothing to do with planets. Most are lopsided or complicated in shape, which is why this near-perfect sphere caught the attention of astronomers George Jacoby of WIYN Observatory, Gary Ferland of the University of Kentucky and Kirk Korista of Western Michigan University.
The team selected it for study precisely because of that unusual symmetry. The nebula measures about five light-years across, while its shell is only about a third of a light-year thick.

understand.summary: The WIYN 3.5-meter Telescope took this through a single blue-green filter that isolates light emitted by oxygen atoms at 500.7 nanometers. The source does not describe how the image was colored.
understand.eye: A long telescope exposure gathers far more light than the eye, and the filter records only one narrow color of light from oxygen.

explore: The picture was taken in 1997 at Kitt Peak National Observatory near Tucson, using the 3.5-m (138-inch) telescope of the WIYN Observatory. It was the subject of a press release at the 197th meeting of the American Astronomical Society in January 2001.
alt: A round shell of gas set among stars.
